# Writing the piece

Before you write, ask the user for what you are missing. The user's request is never everything the user knows. Send one message with at most six questions, the most useful first. Ask only what would change the piece and what the request does not already answer. Look for these:

- **What the reader gets and what it costs them.** The terms as they touch this reader: pay, price, dates, what they keep, what they lose, what they can still do if they change their mind.
- **What answers the reader's main objection.** Name the objection this reader will raise and ask what the user has that answers it: what has already been done or offered about it, what has changed since, what the proposal leaves in place.
- **What shows the writer can deliver, or knows the reader's world.** A record, a credential, a time they did this before, someone who has checked their work or will vouch for it.
- **What the writer can commit to.** A date, a number, a named person, what happens if it is missed.
- **The reader.** Who exactly reads this, what they already think of the writer, and anything they hold against the writer, when the request does not say.
- **The names and dates the piece cannot go out without.** Who it is addressed to, who signs it, a deadline.
- **What the reader will find out anyway.** Close with one open question: is there a cost, a limit, a weak number or a past failure that the request leaves out and this reader knows or will learn?

When the answers come back, write the piece as you normally would, and hand it over. When the user does not know something, write without it and do not guess.

Happy to help. You've already given me a lot, so I just have a few questions. First, though, I'd push back on one point.

**The "ready to publish in a top journal" claim.** I'd advise against it. Marine ecology faculty will know what a top-journal paper needs. This is one season at one bay, it hasn't been repeated, one site lost three months of data, and so far it's only been a poster. A reader who notices that gap may start doubting the rest of the letter, including the parts that are completely true. A stronger move is to make claims they can't argue with: the finding is real and interesting, she designed and carried out the study herself, and with a second year of data it could become a solid paper. You could also say she handled the storm gap well, if she did. If you still want a publication claim after reading the draft, I can phrase it as "I expect this work to lead to a publication." Committees take that seriously, and it holds up.

**Questions (the most useful first):**

1. **How did she handle problems?** When the storm wiped out a site's data, what did she do? More generally, what did you see her decide or work out on her own? One specific story like this will do more for her than any adjective.
2. **How does she compare to the ~30 thesis students you've supervised?** For example, "the best in 17 years" or "top three." This is the line committees look for first.
3. **What did the shellfish lab say about her?** Do you know her supervisor's view, or did she get rehired or asked back? Even one detail helps.
4. **Which courses did she take with you,** and which two did she top? Also, did she do anything beyond the grades, like TA, lead discussions, or ask questions that changed how you taught?
5. **Is there anything a committee would want explained?** For example, a weak grade, little statistics or coding training, or a gap. If there is, I can address it briefly so it doesn't look hidden.
6. **What should I put in the header and signature?** Your name, title, and college, her full name, and whether the letter should be addressed to specific programs or to "Dear Admissions Committee."

If you don't know some of these, that's fine. I'll leave those parts out rather than guess.

I left out anything you didn't confirm, including a story about the storm gap and course names. I also named the study's limits briefly. Committees will see them in her application anyway, and naming them first makes the publication line more believable.

<final_document>
Dr. Anne Caldwell
Department of Biology
Westbrook College
[Email] · [Phone]

[Date]

Dear Admissions Committee,

I am writing to recommend Priya Nair for doctoral study in marine ecology. I have taught biology at Westbrook College for 17 years and supervised about 30 senior theses. Priya is one of the three best students I have taught in that time.

Priya took three courses with me. In two of them, she earned the top grade in a class of 28.

Her senior thesis is where she stood out most. She wanted to know whether oyster growth varies across our bay, so she tracked six sites for 14 months. She did all of the fieldwork herself, which took about 90 trips by kayak through every season. Few full-time undergraduates could keep up that schedule for over a year. She did. Her data show faster growth at the two sites nearest the salt marsh, a pattern well worth following up. She presented the work as a poster at a regional conference.

The study has the limits of a first project. It covers a single period, it has not yet been repeated, and a storm cost one site three months of data. A second season would put the salt-marsh result on firmer ground, and I expect this work to lead to a publication.

Others who have worked with her in the field think as highly of her as I do. Last summer she was a paid field assistant at a state shellfish laboratory. Her supervisor told me he would hire her again. For two weeks, he trusted her to run the lab's water sampling on her own.

Priya already knows what field ecology demands: long seasons, bad weather, lost data, and the discipline to keep going anyway. She has shown she can meet those demands as an undergraduate. I recommend her without reservation and would be glad to answer any questions. Please contact me at [email] or [phone].

Sincerely,

Dr. Anne Caldwell
[Title], Department of Biology
Westbrook College
</final_document>

Before you send it:
- **Fill in the brackets:** your title, email, phone and the date. I didn't guess your academic rank.
- **The storm gap:** if Priya can tell you in a sentence how she handled it (for example, whether she adjusted her analysis), adding that to the limits paragraph would make it one of the letter's strongest points.
- **Course names:** adding them after "three courses with me" would help, especially if any were in ecology or statistics.
